claims.text: GeoDeploy pairs TypeSafe Jev's confidence-scored decisions with the Pulumi Automation API to place and scale Kubernetes across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
GeoDeploy (github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy) is released as open source and is available today.
The GitHub repository https://github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy exists and contains the GeoDeploy example.
The Pulumi Automation API docs exist at /docs/iac/automation-api/.
TypeSafe Jev documentation exists at https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction.
The Pulumi Automation API page exists at /automation/.
TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, its SystemOne model, in the week before this post was published (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's 'SystemOne' model, and access to Jev is currently by early access.
TypeSafe's Jev comes with a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no ('noul') questions, exposed as the `score()`, `choice()`, and `noul()` primitives.
Jev's decision-making primitives are a 'powerful' and 'perfect complement' to agentic work.
Combining Jev's reasoning with Pulumi means the gap between dreaming up ideal infrastructure and deploying it to production 'practically vanishes'.
Agents can now handle infrastructure provisioning and day-to-day scaling and reliability decisions, whereas in the past more choices meant more complexity and technical debt.

A GeoDeploy deployment request has four parts: target geos (locations, traffic share, and data-residency rule), an image (container image and platforms), a workload shape (replicas, CPU and memory per pod, egress, storage), and constraints (allowed providers, max number of providers, budget).
GeoDeploy's data-residency rule options for a target geo are EU-only, US-only, or in-country.
GeoDeploy's image input specifies the platforms the container image is built for: amd64, arm64, or both.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one for each geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.

In GeoDeploy's division of labor, the TypeScript app takes the request, fetches live pricing and does all the math (making no judgment calls); Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use (never doing arithmetic, generating code, or inventing region names); Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS (deciding nothing).
GeoDeploy normalizes each business region (geo) to a canonical location and residency class.
GeoDeploy enumerates every region with managed Kubernetes and uses great-circle distance as its coverage measure.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, and normalizes them into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy uses deterministic TypeScript to bin-pack pods onto nodes, filter out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and compute a monthly cost for each candidate.
GeoDeploy composes a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one Pulumi stack per region.
GeoDeploy will not provision anything unless the user's cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a `plan.json` and a `plan.md` containing the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Unlike a general-purpose LLM, Jev does not return free text; it returns typed answers with calibrated confidence.
Jev returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives: `choice()`, `score()`, and `noul()`.
Jev's `choice()` primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's `score()` primitive rates something against a rubric you describe, and GeoDeploy uses 10 rubric levels.
Jev's `noul()` primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.

Jev only selects from closed sets (region IDs GeoDeploy has already priced and checked), never writes code or does arithmetic, so a hallucinated region such as `us-west-9` or a made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction; Jev cannot answer with a region that isn't on the list.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates along with the constraints and the image's architecture.

GeoDeploy asks Jev, in a single call per geo, for one region selection (`choice`), five quality scores (`score`: coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks (`noul`: data residency satisfied, enough capacity), and a fallback region (`choice`).
The GeoDeploy repository contains the file `packages/decide/src/questions.ts` with a `buildStageAQuestions` function that builds the Jev questions.
The `@typesafe-ai/sdk` package exports `choice`, `noul`, and `score`.

The TypeSafe SDK provides a `TypeSafeClient` class whose `systemOne({ state, questions })` method returns a result with `answers`, where each answer exposes `.choice`, `.confidence`, `.noul`, or `.score` fields (e.g. `a.selection.choice`, `a.selection.confidence`, `a.residencyOk.noul`, `a.coverage.score`).
TypeSafe advises rubric authors to 'describe situations, not degrees', and GeoDeploy's rubrics follow that advice.

Each of GeoDeploy's 10 coverage rubric levels is a concrete scenario, ranging from 'Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence' to 'In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center.'
GeoDeploy's ranking runs on weight profiles: latency-optimized (the default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because the ranking weights live in code, GeoDeploy can re-tune the ranking without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy's weight profiles are: latency-optimized {cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12}; balanced {0.25, 0.25, 0.2, 0.12, 0.18}; residency-first {0.12, 0.12, 0.38, 0.23, 0.15}; failure-domain {0.08, 0.17, 0.48, 0.15, 0.12}.
In GeoDeploy's composite ranking score, sprawl risk is subtracted while cost fit, coverage, maturity, and architecture consistency are added.
Every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.

In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS always means EKS and ECR), and Jev decides only ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier via a second, smaller set of questions.
GeoDeploy checks every Jev answer against a confidence threshold matched to the risk of the decision.
In GeoDeploy, the data-residency check has a confidence threshold of 0.95, and failing it causes a hard reject of the AI region selection.
In GeoDeploy, the region choice for a new cluster requires 0.90 confidence; if it doesn't pass, the top three candidates are flagged for a human to choose.
In GeoDeploy, the region choice when a stack already exists requires 0.75 confidence; if it doesn't pass, the existing region is kept.
In GeoDeploy, an ingress or autoscaling module choice requires 0.85 confidence; if it doesn't pass, the registry default is used.
In GeoDeploy, the node-pool sizing tier choice requires 0.60 confidence; if it doesn't pass, the bin-packing result is used.
In GeoDeploy, region pick, residency, and capacity answers share a global confidence floor of 0.50; below it, the AI path is dropped for that geo.
The GeoDeploy residency check code shown is from `packages/decide/src/engine.ts`.
GeoDeploy enforces confidence gates with plain deterministic code, including a validation that the model's selection is one of the shortlisted candidates.
Each `AiPathAborted` error in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so even a rejected answer ends up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or returns an error, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing the residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.
GeoDeploy's self-driving mode is enabled with the `geodeploy monitor` command.

In self-driving mode, GeoDeploy periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options `no-change`, `scale-up:<geo>`, `scale-down:<geo>`, or `shift:<from>-><to>`, plus a separate check on disruption risk.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, code (not Jev) computes the actual node-count changes.

In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, above 0.85 Jev confidence the resize is applied automatically; between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for a human to approve; below 0.70 GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.

CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric; once a traffic baseline is established it is usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency, error rates, or application-specific metrics.
With access to Jev and a cloud provider, users can get started with GeoDeploy today.
